title: Week 7 · Block 1 — Files
text:
Warm-up 🔥
⏱️ 10 min
Using your own seq_functions.py from last week:
print(gc_content("ATGCGCGGCC"))
print(count_bases("ATGCGCATG"))
Do they still work? React ✅ or ✋

0–10 min. Anyone whose functions are broken gets help now — files build directly on them.

title: Week 7 · Block 1 — Files
section: Data does not live in your script 📄
text:
Data does not live in your script 📄
sequences = ["ATGC", "GGCA"]   # fine for learning 🙂

Real data: sequences.fasta, 5000 sequences, 400 MB 🐘


Time to read files.

10–25 min. Remind them of week 2: they already explored this file with grep.

title: Week 7 · Block 1 — Files
text:
Reading a file
with open("data/sequences.fasta") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line)


with closes the file for you automatically 🚪
The loop gives you one line at a time — works for huge files too

line = line.strip()   # removes the invisible newline ⚠️

strip() is essential — without it every comparison silently fails.

title: Week 7 · Block 1 — Files
Week 7 · Block 1 — Files
section: Building a dictionary from a file

title: Week 7 · Block 1 — Files
text:
Writing a file 💾
with open("results/report.txt", "w") as out:
    out.write("name\tlength\tGC\n")
    for name, seq in sequences.items():
        out.write(f"{name}\t{len(seq)}\t{gc_content(seq):.2f}\n")

"w" overwrites · "a" appends · \n = new line · \t = tab






Warning


"w" destroys the old file without asking. Same rule as > in bash.

title: Week 7 · Block 1 — Files
text:
Exercise 1: Read and count 📄
⏱️ 15 min · your own screen · react ✅
Create scripts/read_fasta.py:

Open data/sequences.fasta
Count how many lines it has
Count how many are headers
Print both numbers

💡 Bonus: print the longest header

25–40 min. Expect path errors — remind them pwd and that paths are relative to where they RUN python.

title: Week 7 · Block 1 — Files
text:
Exercise 2: Real report 📊
⏱️ 30 min · breakout rooms · switch after 15 min
Extend it into scripts/fasta_report.py:

Load the file into a dictionary {name: sequence}
Import your own functions: from seq_functions import gc_content, count_bases
For each sequence compute length and GC content
Write a tab-separated report into results/report.txt
Print a summary: how many sequences, average length, highest GC 🏆

💡 Bonus: write a second file with only the usable sequences (FASTA format!)

40–75 min. The import works only if both files sit in the same folder — a preview of next week’s modules. Plan B: copy the functions into the script.

title: Week 7 · Block 1 — Files
text:
Wrap-up ✅
with open(path) as f:
    for line in f:
        line = line.strip()

strip() every line ⚠️
"w" writes, "a" appends
Your script now works on real data 🧬

Homework 🏠 Commit the script. Do not commit big data files — .gitignore!

75–80 min. Two rooms share their report.txt on screen.

title: Week 4 · Block 2 — Making decisions
text:
Warm-up 🔥
⏱️ 10 min
lengths = [120, 85, 300, 42]

Print the average length
Print the longest
Add 500 to the list and print the new average


0–10 min. Quick recall of list tools before adding logic on top.

title: Week 4 · Block 2 — Making decisions
text:
Scripts that decide 🚦

“Analyse the sequence only if it is longer than 100 bases.”


length = 120

if length > 100:
    print("Long enough — analysing")

10–25 min. Start from the biological question, then show the syntax.

title: Week 4 · Block 2 — Making decisions
Week 4 · Block 2 — Making decisions
text:
Indentation is the syntax ⚠️
if length > 100:
    print("inside the if")   # 4 spaces — belongs to the if
print("always printed")      # no spaces — outside







Warning


In Python, indentation is not decoration — it is the structure. IndentationError will be your friend. 🤝




Show the error live. Tell them: every Python programmer sees this error weekly.

title: Week 4 · Block 2 — Making decisions
text:
Comparing things



Operator
Meaning




==
equal (two =!)


!=
not equal


> < >= <=
bigger / smaller


in
contains



seq == "ATG"          # comparison
seq = "ATG"           # assignment ⚠️ different thing!
"TAG" in seq          # True / False

title: Week 4 · Block 2 — Making decisions
Week 4 · Block 2 — Making decisions
Week 4 · Block 2 — Making decisions
text:
Exercise 2: Sequence quality check 🔬
⏱️ 25 min · breakout rooms · switch after 10 min
Create scripts/seq_check.py. For one sequence, print a verdict:

If it is shorter than 30 bases → "too short"
If it contains an N → "contains unknown bases"
If its GC content is above 60% → "GC rich", below 40% → "AT rich", otherwise "balanced"
If it starts with ATG and its length divides by 3 (len(seq) % 3 == 0) → "possible ORF"

💡 Bonus: test your script on 3 different sequences by changing the variable. Does every rule fire?

35–70 min. % (modulo) is new — explain briefly: remainder after division. Ask pairs to swap sequences with another room to test each other’s scripts.

title: Week 4 · Block 2 — Making decisions
text:
Wrap-up ✅

if / elif / else — one branch wins 🚦
Indentation defines what belongs where
== compares, = assigns ⚠️
and or not in

Homework 🏠 Commit seq_check.py.

Next week: loops — do it for all 500 sequences 🔁

70–80 min. Exit ticket: “What is the difference between = and ==?”

title: Week 5 · Block 2 — Putting it together
text:
Today: no new syntax 🎉
Today we only use what you already know:

variables and types
strings and slicing 🧬
lists 📋
if / elif / else 🚦
for loops 🔁



Programming is not knowing more commands. It is combining few commands well.


0–5 min. Say this explicitly — students often think they are “behind” because they know “only” 5 things.

title: Week 5 · Block 2 — Putting it together
text:
Warm-up: find the bugs 🐛
⏱️ 15 min · pairs · 3 bugs
sequences = ["ATGC", "GGCA", "TTA"]
lengths = []

for seq in sequences
    lengths.append(len(seq))
if len(seq) = 4:
        print("four bases")

print(sum(lenghts))

5–20 min. Bugs: missing colon; = instead of ==; typo lenghts; plus the if is outside the loop. Debugging together is where error messages stop being scary.

title: Week 5 · Block 2 — Putting it together
section: How to attack a bigger task 🧗
text:
How to attack a bigger task 🧗

Say it in words first: “for each sequence, if it is long enough, keep it”
Write it as comments, then fill in the code
Solve it for one element, then wrap it in a loop
print() early and often — see what is actually happening 👀


# for each sequence
#   calculate GC
#   if GC > 0.5, add to the list

20–30 min. This is the actual skill of the course — the rest is syntax.

title: Week 5 · Block 2 — Putting it together
text:
Exercise: Mini analysis 🧬
⏱️ 35 min · breakout rooms · switch after 15 min
sequences = ["ATGCGCTA", "GGC", "ATGGGCCCTAAA", "TTANNNGC", "ATGAAATTTGGG"]
Write scripts/mini_analysis.py that prints a small report:

Total number of sequences and total number of bases
For each sequence: its length, GC content and whether it starts with ATG
How many sequences are “usable” (longer than 5 bases and no N)
The longest sequence and its codons, one per line
A final line: "X of Y sequences passed"

💡 Bonus: put a # comment above each section explaining what it does

30–65 min. Visit every room. Give hints as questions: “what do you want to have at the end?”. Remind them of the empty-list-append pattern if they freeze.

title: Week 5 · Block 2 — Putting it together
text:
Show your work 👀
⏱️ 10 min
Two or three rooms share their screen:

What does your output look like?
Where did you get stuck?
Did anyone solve something differently? 🤔


65–75 min. Praise different solutions — there is no single right one. This also shows AI-generated uniformity is not the goal.

title: Week 5 · Block 2 — Putting it together
text:
Wrap-up ✅
You can now write a real analysis script 🎉
Homework 🏠

Commit mini_analysis.py
Add 2 sequences of your own and check the report still works


Next week: dictionaries and functions — organising data and code 📖

75–80 min. Quiz 3 is around this point in the semester — remind them.

title: Week 6 · Block 2 — Functions
text:
Warm-up 🔥
⏱️ 10 min
seq = "ATGCGCATG"
Count each base using a dictionary and print the result.

Did you write this code before? Where? 🤔

0–10 min. The point: they have written GC content at least three times by now.

title: Week 6 · Block 2 — Functions
section: You keep writing the same thing 🔁
text:
You keep writing the same thing 🔁
gc1 = (seq1.count("G") + seq1.count("C")) / len(seq1)
gc2 = (seq2.count("G") + seq2.count("C")) / len(seq2)
gc3 = (seq3.count("G") + seq3.count("C")) / len(seq3)

Change the formula → change it in three places. Forget one → silent bug 🐛

10–25 min. Silent bugs are worse than crashes — you get a wrong number, not an error.

title: Week 6 · Block 2 — Functions
text:
Defining a function
def gc_content(sequence):
    gc = sequence.count("G") + sequence.count("C")
    return gc / len(sequence)
print(gc_content("ATGCGC"))
print(gc_content(seq2))

def name(input) → return output 📦

title: Week 6 · Block 2 — Functions
text:
Anatomy of a function
def gc_content(sequence, as_percent=False):   # parameters
    gc = sequence.count("G") + sequence.count("C")
    result = gc / len(sequence)
    if as_percent:
        result = result * 100
    return result                              # gives the value back
gc_content("ATGC")                  # 0.5
gc_content("ATGC", as_percent=True) # 50.0

Default arguments are optional to teach — but students love them once they see them.

title: Week 6 · Block 2 — Functions
text:
return is not print ⚠️
def bad(seq):
    print(len(seq))      # shows it, gives nothing back

def good(seq):
    return len(seq)      # gives a value you can USE

total = good("ATGC") + good("GGC")   # works ✅
total = bad("ATGC") + bad("GGC")     # TypeError 🚫

This is THE function misconception. Show the TypeError live and read it together.

title: Week 6 · Block 2 — Functions
text:
Why functions? 🧰

Write once, use everywhere
Name the idea: gc_content() explains itself 📖
Test one small thing instead of a 100-line script
Fix a bug in one place



A good function does one thing and has a clear name.

title: Week 6 · Block 2 — Functions
text:
Exercise 1: Predict, then run 🔮
⏱️ 10 min · chat first
def double(x):
    return x * 2

def shout(text):
    print(text.upper())

print(double(5))
print(double("AT"))
result = shout("atg")
print(result)        # 🤔

25–35 min. The last line printing None is the lesson of the day.

title: Week 6 · Block 2 — Functions
text:
Exercise 2: Your own toolkit 🧰
⏱️ 25 min · breakout rooms · switch after 10 min
Create scripts/seq_functions.py with four functions:

gc_content(seq) → returns GC as a percentage, rounded to 2 decimals
reverse_complement(seq) → returns the reverse complement
count_bases(seq) → returns a dictionary of base counts
is_usable(seq, min_length=30) → returns True/False (long enough and no N)

Then test all four on 3 different sequences and print the results.
💡 Bonus: write longest_orf_start(seq) returning the position of the first ATG, or -1

35–70 min. Most rooms will reuse code from weeks 3–5 — that is exactly the point. Praise copy-from-your-own-repo.

title: Week 6 · Block 2 — Functions
text:
Wrap-up ✅
def name(input):
    ...
    return output

return gives a value back, print only shows it ⚠️
One function = one job, with a clear name
Your repo is now a small toolkit 🧰

Homework 🏠 Commit seq_functions.py.

Next week: files — real data from disk 📄

70–80 min. Tell them next week they will finally read the FASTA file from week 2 with Python.

title: Week 8 · Block 1 — Git in teams
text:
Warm-up 🔥
⏱️ 10 min
git status
git log --oneline
How many commits do you have now? Chat the number 🔢

Seven weeks ago this was your first command. 🙂

0–10 min. Celebrate the progress — most will have 15+ commits.

title: Week 8 · Block 1 — Git in teams
text:
Two people, one repository 😬

You edit seq_functions.py. Your partner edits seq_functions.py. Who wins?


Answer: nobody has to lose — that is what branches are for 🌿

10–25 min. This block is the foundation of the pair assignment.

title: Week 8 · Block 1 — Git in teams
text:
Branches 🌿
git branch                    # where am I?
git switch -c add-gc-function # create and go to a new branch
# ... work, add, commit ...
git switch main               # back to the main line

A branch is a parallel version of your project. Experiment freely — main stays safe. 🛟

title: Week 8 · Block 1 — Git in teams
text:
Sharing a repository 🤝
One of you owns the repo, the other becomes a collaborator:
Repo → Settings → Collaborators → Add people

git clone <url>        # the partner clones it
git pull               # get the newest changes 📥






Note


Golden rule: git pull before you start working. Every time. 🌅

title: Week 8 · Block 1 — Git in teams
text:
Pull requests 📬
git push -u origin add-gc-function
Then on GitHub: Compare & pull request

A pull request is a proposal: “here is my change, please look at it before it goes into main” 👀

Emphasise: this is exactly how professional teams work, including at my job.

title: Week 8 · Block 1 — Git in teams
text:
Code review 👀
On the Files changed tab you can comment on any line.
Good review comments:

“What happens here if the sequence is empty?” 🤔
“Could this be a function? It repeats below”
“Nice — I didn’t know about .get()” 🎉


Review is about the code, never about the person. 💛

Model one good and one bad comment. Online, tone in writing matters even more.

title: Week 8 · Block 1 — Git in teams
text:
Exercise: Your first pull request 📬
⏱️ 35 min · breakout rooms · pairs

A creates a repo pair-assignment and adds B as collaborator
B clones it
Each creates their own branch: git switch -c <yourname>-function
Each writes one small function in a separate file and pushes it
Each opens a pull request and reviews the partner’s one 👀
Merge both pull requests on GitHub


25–65 min. Paste the steps in the chat. Expect authentication issues for B — have the token/gh login plan ready. Visit every room; PR merging is where people get lost.

title: Week 8 · Block 1 — Git in teams
text:
Wrap-up ✅



Command
What it does




git switch -c name
New branch 🌿


git switch main
Go back


git pull
Get partner’s changes 📥


git push -u origin name
Publish your branch



Next block: what happens when you both edit the same line 💥

65–80 min. Leave them curious about conflicts — it is the best part of week 8.

title: Week 2 · Block 1 — The terminal
text:
Warm-up 🔥
⏱️ 10 min · in the chat

Open your terminal and go into your programming-basics folder
Run:

git log --oneline

How many commits do you have? Write the number in the chat 🔢


0–10 min. Quick check who managed the homework. If someone has 0 commits — pair them with someone who has 2.

title: Week 2 · Block 1 — The terminal
text:
Why the terminal? 💻


Clicking

Rename 300 files → 300 × click
“Which files did I already process?”
Impossible to repeat exactly


Terminal

One line for 300 files
The command is the record of what you did
Runs on the server where your data lives 🧬



10–25 min: new material. Mention: sequencing data lives on remote servers — there is no mouse there.

title: Week 2 · Block 1 — The terminal
text:
Where am I? 🗺️
The file system is a tree — you are always standing somewhere in it.
pwd          # print working directory — where am I?
ls           # list — what is here?
ls -l        # long: size, date
ls -a        # all: also hidden files (.git!)

Show that .git is a hidden folder — that’s where the whole history lives.

title: Week 2 · Block 1 — The terminal
text:
Moving around 🚶
cd kse           # go into a folder
cd ..            # one level UP
cd ~             # go home
cd -             # back to where I was

Tab ⇥ completes names · ↑ repeats the last command

Insist on Tab — it is the single biggest quality-of-life improvement for beginners, and it prevents typos.

title: Week 2 · Block 1 — The terminal
text:
Exercise 1: Find your way 🧭
⏱️ 10 min · your own screen · react ✅ when done

pwd — where are you now?
Go home: cd ~
ls — what folders do you see?
Go into your programming-basics folder
ls -a — can you find the .git folder?
Go one level up, then back — using Tab at least once

💡 Bonus: what does ls -lh show that ls -l doesn’t?

25–35 min. Paste steps in the chat. Watch reactions; anyone with ✋ shares their screen.

title: Week 2 · Block 1 — The terminal
text:
Making and moving things 🧰
mkdir data              # make a folder
touch notes.txt         # make an empty file
cp notes.txt backup.txt # copy
mv notes.txt data/      # move (also = rename!)
rm backup.txt           # delete







Warning


rm does not use a trash bin. Deleted is deleted. 💀




Tell a short real story about deleting something important. Then: this is exactly why we use Git.

title: Week 2 · Block 1 — The terminal
text:
Looking inside files 👀
head sequences.fasta      # first 10 lines
head -n 3 sequences.fasta # first 3 lines
tail sequences.fasta      # last 10 lines
less sequences.fasta      # scroll (q = quit!)
wc -l sequences.fasta     # count lines

In less: space = next page, q = quit 🙂

Everyone gets stuck in less at least once. Say “q” twice.

title: Week 2 · Block 1 — The terminal
text:
Exercise 2: Build a project 🏗️
⏱️ 25 min · breakout rooms · one shares the screen, switch after 10 min
Inside programming-basics:

Create folders: data, scripts, results
In data, create a file sample.txt and put 3 lines of text in it (use nano sample.txt, then Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X)
Check with head and wc -l that it has 3 lines
Copy it to results/sample_copy.txt
Rename the copy to results/backup.txt
git add → git commit → git push

💡 Bonus: what happens in Git with the empty scripts folder? Why?

35–70 min. The bonus is a great discussion: Git tracks files, not folders — empty folders never appear on GitHub. Plan B for nano trouble: create the file in VS Code / any editor.

title: Week 2 · Block 1 — The terminal
text:
What we learned ✅



Command
What it does




pwd ls cd
Where am I, what’s here, move


mkdir touch
Make folders and files


cp mv rm
Copy, move/rename, delete


head tail less wc
Look inside, count




Next block: making these commands work together on real DNA data 🧬

70–80 min. Two students share their screen and show their folder structure on GitHub.

title: Week 1 · Block 2 — first commit
text:
Warm-up 🔥 (5 min)
Have you ever had files like this?
thesis.docx
thesis_final.docx
thesis_final_v2.docx
thesis_final_v2_REALLY_FINAL.docx
thesis_final_v2_REALLY_FINAL_fixed_by_supervisor.docx

Write in the chat: which one is the real one? 🤔

0–10 min. Quick laugh + chat discussion. Lead to the question: how do we keep history without chaos?

title: Week 1 · Block 2 — first commit
section: Git = a lab notebook for your files 📓
text:
Git = a lab notebook for your files 📓


Lab notebook

Date of every experiment
What you changed and why
You never tear out pages


Git

Commit = a dated snapshot
Message = what & why
History is never lost

title: Week 1 · Block 2 — first commit
text:
Three words for today



Word
Meaning




Repository (repo)
A project folder with its whole history


Commit
A saved snapshot + a message


GitHub
A website that stores your repo online




Git ≠ GitHub. Git is the tool, GitHub is where we keep the copy.

10–25 min block of “something new”. Keep it under 15 min total.

title: Week 1 · Block 2 — first commit
text:
Exercise 1: First repository 🐙
⏱️ 15 min

On GitHub click New repository → name it programming-basics
✅ Add a README file → Create repository
Click ✏️ on README.md and add:

   # Programming Basics
   My name is ... and I study ...

Write a message → Commit changes
Click History 🕒 — what do you see?

✅ React when you see your commit · 💡 Bonus: make a second change and compare

25–40 min. Everyone works on their own screen, you watch the reactions; ask anyone with ✋ to share their screen.

title: Week 1 · Block 2 — first commit
text:
Opening the terminal 💻

Windows: Git Bash
macOS: Terminal
Linux: Terminal

pwd        # where am I?
ls         # what is here?
cd Desktop # go into a folder
cd ..      # go one level up
mkdir kse  # make a new folder

Live coding: students tell you in the chat what to type. Zoom in the terminal font (Ctrl/Cmd +). Show that typos give errors and that’s fine.

title: Week 1 · Block 2 — first commit
text:
Exercise 2: Find your way (5 min)

Check where you are: pwd
List files: ls
Go to your Desktop (or Documents)
Create a folder kse and go inside it
Check with pwd that you are there ✅

title: Week 1 · Block 2 — first commit
text:
One-time setup ⚙️
Tell Git who you are:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

Use the same e-mail as on GitHub.

Authentication for push: decide beforehand! Options: - GitHub CLI: gh auth login (easiest if installed) - Git Credential Manager (comes with Git for Windows — browser login pops up) - Personal Access Token This step can easily eat 15+ minutes — have a helper or a plan B (web upload).

title: Week 1 · Block 2 — first commit
text:
The Git cycle 🔄

  git clone
  →
  ✏️ edit files
  →
  git add
  →
  git commit
  →
  git push


  ↩️ then back to edit files — again and again


  git clone only once · the blue part every time you work

title: Week 1 · Block 2 — first commit
text:
The commands
# 1. Copy your repo to your laptop (once)
git clone https://github.com/<username>/programming-basics.git
cd programming-basics

# 2. After changing files
git status                     # what changed?
git add about_me.md            # choose what to save
git commit -m "Add about me"   # take the snapshot
git push                       # send it to GitHub

title: Week 1 · Block 2 — first commit
text:
Exercise 3: About me 🎉
⏱️ 20 min · Breakout rooms · one shares the screen and types, one guides — then switch

In the folder kse: git clone your repo, then cd programming-basics
Create about_me.md with: your name, favourite organism 🦠, one thing you want to learn
git status → git add → git commit → git push
Refresh GitHub — is your file there? Post your repo link in the chat 🔗

💡 Bonus: change the file again, make a second commit and look at git log

40–70 min (incl. setup + cycle slides). Paste the steps in the chat before opening rooms. Visit rooms one by one. Biggest risks: authentication on push, cloning into the wrong folder. Plan B for anyone stuck: upload the file via the GitHub website so they still leave with a commit. Plan C if many laptops fail: GitHub Codespaces (terminal in the browser, Git already logged in).

title: Week 1 · Block 2 — first commit
text:
What we did today ✅

Created a repository on GitHub
Used the terminal: pwd, ls, cd, mkdir
Made our first commit and push



From now on, every class ends with a commit.

title: Week 1 · Block 2 — first commit
text:
Cheat sheet 📌



Command
What it does




git clone <url>
Copy a repo to your laptop


git status
Show what changed


git add <file>
Choose files to save


git commit -m "..."
Save a snapshot


git push
Send commits to GitHub


git log
Show history

title: Week 1 · Block 2 — first commit
text:
Before next week 🏠

Make one more commit: add a file expectations.md — what do you want to be able to do in 14 weeks?
Make sure your terminal works on your laptop


Next week: terminal & Bash — working with real FASTA files 🧬

70–80 min. Ask 2 students to share their screen and show their repo. Exit question in the chat: “Write the Git cycle from memory.”

title: Week 2 · Block 2 — Bash on real data
text:
Warm-up 🔥
⏱️ 10 min · in the chat
You are in programming-basics. What does each command do?
cd ../..
ls -a
wc -l data/sample.txt
rm -r results

Careful with the last one — what would you lose? 💀

0–10 min. Predict-then-run: ask for answers in the chat BEFORE anyone runs them.

title: Week 2 · Block 2 — Bash on real data
text:
Our data: FASTA 🧬
>seq1 Homo sapiens BRCA1 partial
ATGGATTTATCTGCTCTTCGCGTTGAAGAAGTACAAAATGTCATTAATGC
>seq2 Mus musculus Brca1 partial
ATGGATTTATCTGCTGTTCGCGTTGAAGAAGTACAAAATGTCATTAATGC

Header lines start with >
Sequence lines are the DNA itself


Download sequences.fasta into your data/ folder — link in the chat 🔗

10–25 min. Put the raw GitHub link in the chat, e.g. the data/ folder of the course repo. Alternative: curl -O <link> — nice, but only if their network cooperates.

title: Week 2 · Block 2 — Bash on real data
text:
Searching: grep 🔎
grep ">" sequences.fasta        # only header lines
grep -c ">" sequences.fasta     # COUNT them = number of sequences
grep -i "brca" sequences.fasta  # ignore upper/lower case
grep -v ">" sequences.fasta     # everything EXCEPT headers

-c = count · -i = ignore case · -v = invert

grep -c ">" is the classic “how many sequences do I have” one-liner. Make sure everyone sees it work.

title: Week 2 · Block 2 — Bash on real data
text:
Pipes: | 🔗
The output of one command becomes the input of the next.
grep -v ">" sequences.fasta | wc -l    # how many sequence lines?
grep ">" sequences.fasta | head -n 3   # first 3 headers


Small tools, combined. That is the whole idea of the terminal.


Analogy: a pipeline in the lab — each step passes the sample to the next step.

title: Week 2 · Block 2 — Bash on real data
text:
Saving results: > 💾
grep ">" sequences.fasta > headers.txt     # write to a file
grep ">" sequences.fasta >> headers.txt    # ADD to a file







Warning


> overwrites the file without asking. >> adds at the end.

title: Week 2 · Block 2 — Bash on real data
text:
Exercise: Explore the data 🧬
⏱️ 25 min · breakout rooms · switch who types after 10 min

How many sequences are in sequences.fasta?
Save all headers into results/headers.txt
How many lines are not headers?
Find all sequences from Homo sapiens — how many?
Show the first 2 headers only (use a pipe)

💡 Bonus: what does this do, and why is the number different from question 1?
grep -c "ATG" sequences.fasta

25–60 min. Paste the questions in the chat before opening rooms. Bonus discussion: grep counts LINES containing ATG, not occurrences — a classic bioinformatics trap.

title: Week 2 · Block 2 — Bash on real data
text:
Back to Git: .gitignore 🙈
Some files should never go to GitHub:

huge data files 🐘
results you can regenerate
passwords and tokens 🔑

nano .gitignore
results/
*.fasta

Warning: .gitignore only works on files Git is not tracking yet 😉

60–70 min. Tell them this is exactly the mistake I made with these slides — rendered files ended up on GitHub.

title: Week 2 · Block 2 — Bash on real data
text:
Wrap-up ✅



Command
What it does




grep "x" file
Find lines containing x


grep -c -i -v
Count · ignore case · invert


cmd1 \| cmd2
Pipe: output → input


> file >> file
Save · append



Homework 🏠 Add .gitignore to your repo, commit and push.

Next week: Python 🐍

70–80 min. Ask 2 students to share their screen with the answer to question 4. Exit ticket in the chat: one command they will actually use again.

title: Week 6 · Block 1 — Dictionaries
text:
Warm-up 🔥
⏱️ 10 min
sequences = ["ATGC", "GGCATT", "TTA"]
Write a loop that prints only the sequences longer than 3 bases.

0–10 min. Quick recall. Two volunteers share their screen.

title: Week 6 · Block 1 — Dictionaries
text:
The problem with lists 😩
names   = ["seq1", "seq2", "seq3"]
lengths = [120, 85, 300]
To find the length of seq2 you must find its position first. 😖

What if the two lists get out of sync? 💥

10–25 min. This “parallel lists” trap is common in beginner scripts — make the pain visible.

title: Week 6 · Block 1 — Dictionaries
text:
Dictionaries: key → value 📖
lengths = {"seq1": 120, "seq2": 85, "seq3": 300}

lengths["seq2"]           # 85 — look up by NAME, not position
lengths["seq4"] = 42      # add a new entry
len(lengths)              # 4

Keys are unique · values can be anything 🔑

title: Week 6 · Block 1 — Dictionaries
text:
Looping over a dictionary
for name in lengths:
    print(name, lengths[name])

for name, value in lengths.items():
    print(f"{name} has {value} bases")

"seq1" in lengths       # True — checks the KEYS
lengths.get("seq9", 0)  # 0 instead of an error 🛟

.get() saves them from KeyError, the most common dictionary bug.

title: Week 6 · Block 1 — Dictionaries
Week 6 · Block 1 — Dictionaries
text:
Exercise 1: Predict, then run 🔮
⏱️ 10 min · chat first
d = {"A": 1, "T": 2}
d["G"] = 3
d["A"] = d["A"] + 10

print(len(d))
print(d["A"])
print("C" in d)
print(d.get("C", 0))

25–35 min. Highlight the difference between the last two lines.

title: Week 6 · Block 1 — Dictionaries
text:
Exercise 2: Codon counter 🧬
⏱️ 25 min · breakout rooms · switch after 10 min
Create scripts/codon_count.py:
seq = "ATGCGCATGGGCATGTAACGCATG"

Count how many times each base appears (dictionary!)
Print the counts nicely: A: 6, T: 4, …
Now count codons (3-letter chunks) — use range(0, len(seq), 3)
Which codon appears most often? 🏆
Print how many different codons were found

💡 Bonus: store sequences as a dictionary {"seq1": "ATGC", ...} and print the length of each

35–70 min. Point 4 is genuinely hard — hint: loop over the dictionary keeping a “best so far” variable.

title: Week 6 · Block 1 — Dictionaries
text:
Wrap-up ✅



List 📋
Dictionary 📖




Ordered, by position
By key


seqs[0]
lengths["seq1"]


Good for: many similar items
Good for: named values, counting



Homework 🏠 Commit codon_count.py.

Next block: functions — stop repeating yourself 🔁

70–80 min. Exit ticket: one thing from their studies that is naturally a key → value pair.

title: Week 3 · Block 1 — Hello, Python
text:
Warm-up 🔥
⏱️ 10 min · in the chat
In your repo, using one line each:

How many sequences are in data/sequences.fasta?
Save the headers into results/headers.txt


Stuck? Ask your partner first, then the chat 💬

0–10 min. Recall last week. If many struggle, redo the grep pipeline live — it is the base for everything later.

title: Week 3 · Block 1 — Hello, Python
text:
Bash vs Python 🐍


Bash is great for

Moving and filtering files
Gluing tools together
One-liners


Python is great for

Logic and calculations
Reusable analysis
Anything longer than 2 lines 🙂



10–25 min: new material. Do not oppose them — biologists use both, daily.

title: Week 3 · Block 1 — Hello, Python
text:
Two ways to run Python
python3                 # interactive — try things out (exit())
python3 my_script.py    # run a saved script

We use scripts, because a script can be committed, shared and re-run. 💾

Check that everyone actually has python3. Windows users may need python instead.

title: Week 3 · Block 1 — Hello, Python
text:
Your first script
# hello.py
print("Hello, bioinformatics!")
print(2 + 2)
python3 hello.py

# starts a comment — Python ignores it, humans read it.

title: Week 3 · Block 1 — Hello, Python
text:
Variables 📦
organism = "Homo sapiens"
gene_length = 1520
gc_content = 0.42
is_coding = True

print(organism, gene_length)

A variable is a label on a value, not a box you must declare.

title: Week 3 · Block 1 — Hello, Python
text:
Four basic types



Type
Example
Used for




str
"ATGC"
text, sequences


int
1520
counts, positions


float
0.42
ratios, p-values


bool
True / False
yes/no answers



type(gc_content)   # <class 'float'>

Show a classic error: “ATG” + 5 → TypeError. Read the error message together, slowly.

title: Week 3 · Block 1 — Hello, Python
text:
Exercise 1: Predict, then run 🔮
⏱️ 10 min · answer in the chat before running
a = 5
b = "5"
print(a + a)
print(b + b)
print(a + b)
💡 Which line fails? What exactly does the error say?

25–35 min. This is the single most useful habit: read the error, don’t panic.

title: Week 3 · Block 1 — Hello, Python
text:
Input and conversion
length = input("Sequence length: ")   # always a STRING
length = int(length)                  # convert to number
print(length * 3)

int() · float() · str() convert between types.

title: Week 3 · Block 1 — Hello, Python
text:
Exercise 2: Your first analysis 🧬
⏱️ 25 min · breakout rooms · switch after 10 min
Create scripts/dna_info.py:

Store a DNA sequence in a variable (at least 20 letters)
Print its length using len(sequence)
Count the G letters: sequence.count("G")
Count the C letters
Calculate and print the GC content as a percentage
git add → commit → push

💡 Bonus: print the result rounded: round(value, 2)

35–70 min. Paste in the chat. Common bug: integer division confusion — remind them / gives a float.

title: Week 3 · Block 1 — Hello, Python
text:
Wrap-up ✅

A script is a file you can re-run and commit 💾
Variables hold values; values have types
len() count() already do real biology work

Homework 🏠 Commit dna_info.py with a comment at the top explaining what it does.

Next block: strings — sequences are just text 🧬

70–80 min. Two students share their GC result — compare numbers, discuss why they differ.

title: Week 5 · Block 1 — Loops
text:
Warm-up 🔥
⏱️ 10 min
seq = "ATGCCCTAAGGG"
Write an if that prints "start codon found" when the sequence starts with ATG and is longer than 6 bases.

0–10 min. Two students share their screen with different solutions.

title: Week 5 · Block 1 — Loops
text:
The problem 😩
print(len(sequences[0]))
print(len(sequences[1]))
print(len(sequences[2]))
# ... 497 more lines


Copy-paste is a smell. Computers are good at repeating things. 🔁


10–25 min. Reference last week’s exercise where they wrote lengths by hand.

title: Week 5 · Block 1 — Loops
text:
The for loop
sequences = ["ATGC", "GGCATT", "TTA"]

for seq in sequences:
    print(seq, len(seq))

Read it as: for each seq in sequences, do this.
seq is just a name — you choose it.

title: Week 5 · Block 1 — Loops
Week 5 · Block 1 — Loops
text:
Collecting results 📋
lengths = []                    # start empty

for seq in sequences:
    lengths.append(len(seq))    # add one result per sequence

print(lengths)
print(sum(lengths) / len(lengths))

Empty list → loop → append. You will write this a hundred times.

title: Week 5 · Block 1 — Loops
text:
range() and while
for i in range(5):        # 0,1,2,3,4
    print(i)

for i in range(0, 9, 3):  # 0,3,6 — codon positions!
    print(seq[i:i+3])

while len(seq) > 3:       # repeat while the condition holds
    seq = seq[1:]






Warning


Forget to change the condition → infinite loop. Ctrl+C stops it. 🛑




Teach Ctrl+C explicitly — online, a student with a runaway loop will panic silently.

title: Week 5 · Block 1 — Loops
text:
Exercise 1: Predict, then run 🔮
⏱️ 10 min · chat first
total = 0
for n in [1, 2, 3, 4]:
    total = total + n
print(total)

for base in "ATG":
    print(base * 2)

25–35 min. If they get the accumulator, the rest of the semester is much easier.

title: Week 5 · Block 1 — Loops
text:
Exercise 2: Analyse them all 🧬
⏱️ 25 min · breakout rooms · switch after 10 min
Create scripts/analyse_all.py:
sequences = ["ATGCGC", "GGCATTAGC", "TTA", "ATGGGCCCTA", "ATGNNNCGC"]

Print each sequence with its length
Build a list of lengths, then print the average
Count how many sequences start with ATG
Print only the sequences longer than 5 bases
For each sequence print its GC content (loop inside a loop!)

💡 Bonus: print the codons of the longest sequence, one per line

35–70 min. Point 5 is the hard one — a loop over sequences containing a loop over bases. Hint to give if a room is stuck: solve it for ONE sequence first, then wrap it in the outer loop.

title: Week 5 · Block 1 — Loops
text:
Wrap-up ✅
results = []
for item in things:
    if condition:
        results.append(something)

for x in y: repeats for each element
Empty list → loop → append 📋
range() for numbers · while for “until”

Homework 🏠 Commit analyse_all.py.

70–80 min. Exit ticket: name one thing from their own studies they would now loop over.

title: Week 3 · Block 2 — Strings are sequences
text:
Warm-up 🔥
⏱️ 10 min
seq = "ATGCGCTA"
print(len(seq))
print(seq.count("A"))
print(seq.count("AT"))
What will each line print? Chat first, run second 💬

0–10 min. The third line surprises people — counting pairs, not letters.

title: Week 3 · Block 2 — Strings are sequences
text:
Indexing: counting from 0 🔢
seq = "ATGCGC"
seq[0]    # 'A'  — the FIRST letter
seq[1]    # 'T'
seq[-1]   # 'C'  — the last one







Note


Biologists count bases from 1, Python counts from 0. This causes real bugs in real papers. 🐛




10–25 min. Mention the classic off-by-one error in genomic coordinates (BED vs GFF).

title: Week 3 · Block 2 — Strings are sequences
text:
Slicing ✂️
seq = "ATGCGCTAGC"
seq[0:3]    # 'ATG'  — from 0 up to (not including) 3
seq[3:]     # from 3 to the end
seq[:3]     # from the start to 3
seq[::-1]   # reversed!

seq[start:stop] — stop is not included 🙂

title: Week 3 · Block 2 — Strings are sequences
text:
Useful string methods
seq.upper()              # 'ATGC'
seq.lower()              # 'atgc'
seq.replace("T", "U")    # DNA → RNA!
seq.count("GC")
seq.find("ATG")          # position of the first ATG (-1 if absent)
seq.startswith(">")      # True / False — FASTA headers!

A method does not change the original — it returns a new string.

Important: seq.upper() alone does nothing unless you assign it. Show the mistake live.

title: Week 3 · Block 2 — Strings are sequences
text:
Building strings
name = "seq1"
length = 42

print("Sequence " + name + " has " + str(length) + " bases")
print(f"Sequence {name} has {length} bases")     # f-string 👑

f-strings are shorter and you don’t need str().

title: Week 3 · Block 2 — Strings are sequences
text:
Exercise 1: Slice it 🔪
⏱️ 10 min · your own screen · react ✅ when done
seq = "ATGGCCATTGTAATGGGCCGC"

Print the first codon (3 letters)
Print the last 6 bases
Print the sequence reversed
Convert it to RNA and print it
At which position does the second ATG start? 🤔


25–35 min. Question 5 is genuinely hard — find has a start argument: seq.find(“ATG”, 1).

title: Week 3 · Block 2 — Strings are sequences
text:
Reverse complement 🧬
The classic first real bioinformatics function:
seq = "ATGC"
complement = seq.replace("A", "t").replace("T", "a")
complement = complement.replace("G", "c").replace("C", "g")
rev_comp = complement.upper()[::-1]
print(rev_comp)

Why the temporary lowercase? 🤔 Try it without — what breaks?

Great discussion: replacing A→T then T→A turns everything into A. The lowercase trick avoids double replacement.

title: Week 3 · Block 2 — Strings are sequences
text:
Exercise 2: Sequence toolkit 🧰
⏱️ 25 min · breakout rooms · switch after 10 min
Create scripts/seq_tools.py. For a DNA sequence of your choice, print:

Its length and GC content (reuse last block’s code)
Its first codon and last codon
The RNA version
The reverse complement
Whether it starts with a start codon (ATG) — print True/False

💡 Bonus: print all three reading frames: seq[0:], seq[1:], seq[2:]

35–70 min. Paste in the chat. Encourage f-strings for nice output — makes results readable.

title: Week 3 · Block 2 — Strings are sequences
text:
Wrap-up ✅



Tool
Example




Index
seq[0] seq[-1]


Slice
seq[0:3] seq[::-1]


Methods
.upper() .replace() .find()


f-string
f"GC = {gc}%"



Homework 🏠 Commit seq_tools.py and write in the README what it does.

Next week: lists — many sequences at once 📋

70–80 min. Exit ticket: “Python counts from ___” in the chat.

title: Week 8 · Block 2 — Conflicts & the pair assignment
text:
Warm-up 🔥
⏱️ 10 min
In your pair-assignment repo:
git switch main
git pull
ls
Do you see your partner’s file? React ✅

0–10 min. This confirms yesterday’s merges actually landed in main.

title: Week 8 · Block 2 — Conflicts & the pair assignment
text:
The moment of truth 💥
You both edited the same line.
<<<<<<< HEAD
gc = round(value, 2)
=======
gc = round(value, 3)
>>>>>>> partner-branch

Git does not guess. You decide. 🧑‍⚖️

10–25 min. Reassure: a conflict is not damage, nothing is lost.

title: Week 8 · Block 2 — Conflicts & the pair assignment
text:
Resolving a conflict 🧑‍⚖️

git status — which files are in conflict?
Open the file, find the <<<<<<< markers
Keep what should stay — delete all markers ✂️
Save, then:

git add <file>
git commit -m "Resolve conflict in seq_functions.py"
git push

VS Code shows buttons: Accept Current / Incoming / Both 🖱️

title: Week 8 · Block 2 — Conflicts & the pair assignment
text:
How to avoid conflicts 🛡️

git pull before you start working 🌅
Small, frequent commits, not one giant one
Agree who works on which file ✋
Talk to each other 💬



Conflicts are a communication problem more than a Git problem.

title: Week 8 · Block 2 — Conflicts & the pair assignment
section: Exercise 1: Make a conflict on purpose 😈
text:
Exercise 1: Make a conflict on purpose 😈
⏱️ 25 min · breakout rooms · pairs

Both of you: git switch main and git pull
Both edit the same line of the same file — differently
Both commit. A pushes first ✅
B pushes → rejected → git pull → 💥 conflict
Resolve it together, commit, push
Both run git log --oneline — do you see the same history?


25–50 min. Doing it deliberately in class is much better than meeting it in panic at 2 a.m.

title: Week 8 · Block 2 — Conflicts & the pair assignment
text:
Pair assignment 📋
25% of your grade · due in 2 weeks · in pairs
Build a small FASTA analysis tool together, in one repository:

At least 4 functions, each written by one of you
Each function on its own branch, merged via a pull request
Each of you reviews at least 2 of your partner’s pull requests 👀
A README.md explaining what it does and how to run it
At least one resolved conflict in the history 😈


50–65 min. Walk through each point. Stress: I grade the collaboration, not only the code.

Part

⏱️ 15 min · breakout rooms · with your partner
Before you leave today, write it in your README.md:

Which 4 functions will your tool have?
Who writes which one? ✋

Wrap-up ✅

Conflicts: keep what should stay, delete the markers ✂️
git pull before starting, always 🌅
Your assignment starts now 📋


Next week: scripts as tools — running your code from the terminal ⚙️

title: Week 7 · Block 2 — Errors & debugging
text:
Warm-up 🔥
⏱️ 10 min · in the chat
What error would you expect from each line?
open("data/sequenses.fasta")
int("ATG")
counts["X"]
"ATG" + 5

0–10 min. They have met all four already. Naming them out loud removes the fear.

title: Week 7 · Block 2 — Errors & debugging
text:
Errors are messages, not failures 💌

Nobody writes code that works the first time. Not me, not your supervisor, not anyone. 🙂


The skill is not avoiding errors. The skill is reading them.

10–25 min. Say this sincerely — online, beginners often feel alone with a red screen.

title: Week 7 · Block 2 — Errors & debugging
text:
How to read a traceback 🔍
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "fasta_report.py", line 14, in <module>
    gc = gc_content(seq)
  File "seq_functions.py", line 3, in gc_content
    return gc / len(sequence)
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero


Bottom line = what went wrong 🎯
Above it = where, and how you got there
Read from the bottom up

title: Week 7 · Block 2 — Errors & debugging
text:
The usual suspects



Error
Usually means




SyntaxError
Missing : ) or quote


IndentationError
Wrong number of spaces


NameError
Typo, or variable not defined yet


TypeError
Mixing text and numbers


KeyError
That key is not in the dictionary


IndexError
Position beyond the end of the list


FileNotFoundError
Wrong path — run pwd 📍

title: Week 7 · Block 2 — Errors & debugging
text:
Debugging with print() 🖨️
for line in f:
    line = line.strip()
    print("DEBUG:", repr(line))    # what is REALLY in there?
    if line.startswith(">"):
        ...

repr() shows the invisible: 'ATGC\n' vs 'ATGC' 👀

Professional debuggers exist — but print() is what everyone actually uses first.

title: Week 7 · Block 2 — Errors & debugging
text:
Silent bugs 🤫
gc = (seq.count("G") + seq.count("C")) / len(seq) * 100
No error. Result: 4200.0 🤨

Ask yourself: does this number make biological sense?

25–35 min. Most dangerous class of bug: wrong results that look fine. Tie back to the AI policy — this is what you cannot catch if you did not write the code.

title: Week 7 · Block 2 — Errors & debugging
text:
Exercise 1: Fix the script 🔧
⏱️ 20 min · breakout rooms · 5 bugs
I will paste scripts/broken_report.py in the chat 📋

Run it and read the first error only
Fix it, run again, repeat
Write in the chat which error types you met

💡 Bonus: one bug produces no error at all. Can you find it? 🤫

35–55 min. Prepare broken_report.py beforehand: missing colon, wrong variable name, missing strip(), KeyError, and one silent maths bug.

title: Week 7 · Block 2 — Errors & debugging
text:
Defensive coding 🛡️
if len(sequence) == 0:
    print("Warning: empty sequence, skipping")
    continue

value = counts.get("N", 0)     # safe lookup

Check your assumptions before the data surprises you.

title: Week 7 · Block 2 — Errors & debugging
text:
Exercise 2: Make it robust 🧪
⏱️ 20 min · pairs
Take your own fasta_report.py and break-proof it:

What happens if the file does not exist? Print a friendly message
What if a sequence is empty? Skip it, don’t crash
What if a sequence contains N? Report how many
Swap scripts with another room and try to break theirs 😈


55–75 min. The swap is the fun part — testing someone else’s code is a real skill.

title: Week 7 · Block 2 — Errors & debugging
text:
Wrap-up ✅

Read tracebacks bottom up 🔍
print() and repr() are your debugger
Ask: does this number make sense? 🤨
Errors are normal — being stuck silently is not 💬

Homework 🏠 Commit your robust version.

Next week: Git in teams — and your pair assignment 👥

75–80 min. Announce the pair assignment explicitly: 25% of the grade, starts next week.

title: Week 1 · Block 1 — Welcome!

Why does a biologist need code?


By hand

1 FASTA file → OK
500 FASTA files → a week of copy & paste
“Which version of the table did I use?” 🤯


With code

500 files → one script, a few seconds
Same result every time
Full history of every change



Keep it short. The goal is motivation, not a lecture.

title: Week 1 · Block 1 — Welcome!
text:
Rules of our online room

🎥 Camera on during pair work, if you can
👥 Pairs: one shares the screen, the other guides — switch every 10 min
✅ Reaction = “it works” · ✋ Raise hand = “I need help”
⏱️ Stuck for more than 5 minutes? Write in the chat
❌ Errors are normal — reading them is a skill we will learn
💾 Every class ends with a commit


Stress the 5-minute rule: online, beginners get stuck silently.

title: Week 1 · Block 1 — Welcome!
text:
Oral exam 💬

15 minutes per person, in the last week of classes
We talk about your final project code
Goal: see what you have learned



This is a conversation, not an interrogation. 🙂



No attendance tracking — but practice in class is where you learn.

Oral exam questions ideas: walk me through your script; why did you use a dictionary here; what would you change; what was the hardest part. Timing: week 14 has 160 min → only ~10 students in class time. Plan extra slots if the group is bigger.

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
text:
Warm-up 🔥
⏱️ 10 min
seq = "ATGCGCTAGCTT"

Print the last 3 bases
Print the RNA version
Print True if it contains "TAG" (hint: in)


0–10 min. "TAG" in seq is new but guessable — let them try before you show it.

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
text:
One sequence is never enough 📋
seq1 = "ATGC"
seq2 = "GGCA"
seq3 = "TTAG"
# ... and 500 more? 😱

sequences = ["ATGC", "GGCA", "TTAG"]

10–25 min. Motivation first: real data comes in hundreds of sequences.

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
text:
Working with lists
sequences = ["ATGC", "GGCA", "TTAG"]

sequences[0]        # 'ATGC' — same indexing as strings!
sequences[-1]       # 'TTAG'
len(sequences)      # 3
sequences[0:2]      # ['ATGC', 'GGCA'] — slicing works too

Lists hold anything: numbers, strings, even other lists.

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
text:
Changing lists ✏️
sequences.append("CCGG")     # add at the end
sequences.insert(0, "AAAA")  # add at a position
sequences.remove("GGCA")     # remove by value
last = sequences.pop()       # remove and return the last one
sequences[0] = "TTTT"        # replace







Note


Strings cannot be changed, lists can. seq[0] = "G" → error 🚫

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
text:
Useful list tools
lengths = [120, 85, 300, 42]

sum(lengths)          # 547
max(lengths)          # 300
min(lengths)          # 42
sorted(lengths)       # [42, 85, 120, 300]
len(lengths)          # 4
sum(lengths) / len(lengths)   # average 🧮

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
section: From string to list and back
text:
From string to list and back
header = ">seq1 Homo sapiens BRCA1"
parts = header.split()        # ['>seq1', 'Homo', 'sapiens', 'BRCA1']
parts[1]                      # 'Homo'

"-".join(["ATG", "CGC"])      # 'ATG-CGC'
list("ATGC")                  # ['A', 'T', 'G', 'C']

split() is how you will parse every data file 📄

Show splitting a CSV line: "seq1,120,0.42".split(","). This is the bridge to real files.

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
text:
Exercise 1: Predict, then run 🔮
⏱️ 10 min · chat first
seqs = ["ATG", "GGC"]
seqs.append("TTA")
print(len(seqs))
print(seqs[1])
print(seqs[1][0])      # 🤔
print(sorted(seqs))

25–35 min. seqs[1][0] is the key idea: indexing a list, then indexing the string inside it.

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
text:
Exercise 2: Sequence statistics 📊
⏱️ 25 min · breakout rooms · switch after 10 min
Create scripts/seq_stats.py:
sequences = ["ATGCGC", "GGCATTAGC", "TTA", "ATGGGCCCTA"]

How many sequences are there?
Print the first and the last one
Add one more sequence of your own
Make a list of their lengths (by hand is fine — 5 values)
Print the longest, shortest and average length
Split this header and print the species: ">seq1 Homo sapiens BRCA1"

💡 Bonus: print the sequences sorted alphabetically

35–70 min. Point 4 by hand is intentional — next block’s loops will feel like a relief.

title: Week 4 · Block 1 — Lists
text:
Wrap-up ✅

Lists hold many values: ["ATG", "GGC"]
Same indexing and slicing as strings
append remove sorted sum max min
split() turns text into a list 📄

Homework 🏠 Commit seq_stats.py.

Next block: decisions — if 🚦

70–80 min. Tease: “next time your script can decide what to do — e.g. skip short sequences”.
